newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RBNZ's Brash could work with slightly wider band.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ's Brash could work with slightly wider band.

text.p: Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash said on Friday he could work with a slightly wider target band for underlying inflation than the current 0-2 percent range.
But he stressed the current band, defined in the policy targets agreement between the governor and Finance Minister Bill Birch, had served New Zealand well.
Opposition parties have indicated they would widen the band if they won office in the October 12 election, with Labour favouring a move to minus one to three percent.
Brash said there was no perfect answer to what the width of the inflation target band should be.
"If it was slightly wider, I don't think it would necessarily be a resignation issue.
"I think there are huge benefits in the present framework and I have yet to be persuaded a wider range would make sense.
"That is not to say it is not an issue which has to be looked at from time to time. Some wider bands I would feel very uncomfortable with, others might be looked at," he said.
"It would depend on the extent of it. It would depend also upon the mid-point of it.

"If the midpoint, for argument's sake, to be absurd, were five percent I'd have much, much greater difficulty trying to reconcile that with the current Act than if the mid-point were to remain at 1.0 (percent)."
He said it was only speculation.
"Nought to two percent has served us well in the past by anchoring inflationary expectations at a very low level.
"It's produced benefits in terms of lower bond yields, lower inflation, lower unemployment and so on.
"I think all of those things have been very valuable to us."
He said he could not reasonably comment on whether he would remain in office after the election.
"My current term runs until September 1998 and the Act quite explicity provides that I can be dismissed for a variety of reasons...one of which is inadequate performance under the inflation target.
"At the moment, with inflation at 2.7 percent it would up to a minister to judge if that is in fact inadequate," Brash said.
Brash issued a veiled threat to political parties favouring greater spending.
He said "a significant change in the fiscal outlook would require some adjustment to monetary policy."
